title: John the Baptist's birth (24 June)
hookLine: six months before Christmas, at midsummer, as days start shortening: he must increase, I decrease

cards: John the Baptist's followers come to him worried. In the King James Bible: "Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all men come to him."
The crowds are leaving. The man John pointed to is drawing everyone, and his river bank is getting quiet. To anyone with a following, that could sound like bad news.
His followers might expect him to be hurt, or to fight back. What John says instead turns the worry inside out. And the church gives him a feast day for being born.

teach.b: "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled."
He casts himself as the best man, whose job is not to be the groom. His joy is standing near and hearing the groom happy.
Then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Not through gritted teeth. As the fulfillment of his joy.

Now the birth, which Luke tells with care. The angel tells Mary that her elderly cousin Elizabeth is expecting too: "this is the sixth month with her." When Mary arrives, "the babe leaped in her womb."
At the birth, the neighbors expect him to be named after his father, Zacharias, who can't speak.
He asks for a writing tablet and writes, "His name is John." Tradition reads Luke's sixth month this way, and the church calendar sets John's birth six months before Christmas.
Some readers notice something in the sky, too.
North of the equator, John's day falls just as the long days of midsummer begin to shorten, and Christmas just as the short days begin to lengthen. The light itself seems to act out his line.
In some places, people light bonfires on the eve of the feast: a celebration for a man remembered for stepping aside.

how: Churches that keep the birth of John the Baptist read Luke's account of his birth and naming, and in some places people mark the eve of the feast with bonfires.

games.q: you're John. your followers tell you the crowds have gone over to Jesus. what do you say?
o: "he must increase, but I must decrease."
games.why: John calls himself the bridegroom's friend, glad to hear his voice: "this my joy therefore is fulfilled."

practice: Bring to mind someone near you who's doing well right now, a colleague getting noticed, a friend whose thing is working, and notice whatever comes up in you without scolding it.

Then try John's posture: the friend who stands near, hears the good news, and is glad. If you pray, thank God for that person's good thing by name; if you don't, wish it bigger for them, and mean it if you can.

wordCard.voice: Bridegroom. John the Baptist's name for Jesus, calling himself only the friend who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice and happily steps back.

orig.note: Greek: to become less. The second half of John's line, I must decrease.

carryVoice: Your line: I must decrease. For John, that was joy, not loss. See you tomorrow.
